title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & benchmark playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material used by the Eng:ServingRuntime team. It combines the runtime architecture overview, kernel-scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, the canonical benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues and mitigations, and operational runbooks used during on-call and incident response. Use this page as the single source of truth for production inference behavior and runbook procedures.

Goals
- Communicate architecture and operator-level expectations.
- Provide reproducible profiling and benchmarking workflows.
- Define scheduling knobs and safe default policies.
- Maintain a short, actionable runbook set for common incidents.

Owner and contacts
- Primary owner: Eng:ServingRuntime (team lead: Maya Chen)
- On-call rotation: serving-runtime-sre@redwood-inference.internal
- Slack channel: #serving-runtime (pager integrations enabled)

SLOs and operational targets
- 99th percentile token latency (hosted): <= 250ms for p50 prompt sizes (<= 512 tokens)
- Throughput SLO (per-dedicated-pool): 15K tokens/s per 8xA100-equivalent GPU pool (commit)
- Error rate SLO: request failures < 0.05% (excl. client errors)
- On-call response: page acknowledged within 15 minutes

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary
The serving runtime is composed of three logical layers: the control plane (routing, policy), the runtime scheduler (kernel selection, batching, KV cache), and the execution layer (device drivers, CUDA/ROCm kernels, quantized ops). The system is designed to: scale horizontally, enforce latency SLOs, and fall back to compatible model variants under contention.

Key components
- API Gateway: auth, rate limiting, and ingress shaping.
- Router: policy-based routing (latency-first, cost-first, region pinning).
- Scheduler: continuous batching engine, KV cache manager, and kernel selector.
- Executor: per-GPU worker processes, memory manager, and low-level optimized kernels (FlashAttention variants, fused MLP matmuls).
- Telemetry: per-token tracing, cost attribution, and perf counters.

Service ownership and interfaces
- Router team: responsible for routing polices and compat matrix.
- Scheduler team: owns batching window, queueing, and kernel heuristics.
- Runtime team: kernel implementations and quantization paths.

2) Kernel scheduling and heuristics

Design goals
- Maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs.
- Select kernels based on model architecture, sequence length distribution, current occupancy, and quantization profile.

Primary heuristics (order of application)
1. Fast-path selection: if sequence length < short_seq_thresh (default 64) and model supports flash kernels, prefer fused attention kernel.
2. Quantization-aware selection: if model is int8/4 and hardware supports int8 GEMM, prefer quantized kernels with fallback microkernels for rare ops.
3. Occupancy fallback: when GPU SM occupancy > occupancy_block_threshold (default 0.91), switch to conservative tiled kernels to reduce memory thrash.
4. KV-cache locality: prefer kernels that minimize host-device data transfer when cache hits exceed 25%.

Config table (defaults)
| param | default | description |
| short_seq_thresh | 64 | tokens under this prefer flash kernels |
| occupancy_block_threshold | 0.91 | SM occupancy fraction to trigger conservative kernels |
| batching_max_delay_ms | 6 | max time to wait to form a batch |
| batching_max_tokens | 16384 | max cumulative tokens per batch |
| kv_cache_elastic_eviction | true | enable elastic eviction for inactive keys |

Tuning advice
- For low-latency real-time apps, set batching_max_delay_ms <= 4 and short_seq_thresh <= 32.
- For high-throughput offline workloads, increase batching_max_delay_ms to 10-20ms and batching_max_tokens to >64K.
- Use the occupancy histogram (see profiling playbook) to tune occupancy_block_threshold per GPU family.

3) Profiling playbook (how to reproduce and act on perf regressions)

When to run profiling
- Token latency regressions observed (p95/p99 drift > 15% from baseline).
- Throughput drop for dedicated pools.
- New kernel or quantization rollout.

Quick checklist
1. Capture a 5-20 minute perf trace using the capture tool: 
   - CLI: ri-profiler capture --pool <pool-id> --duration 300 --trace-level full --out /tmp/run.trace
2. Generate occupancy and kernel timelines: 
   - ri-profiler analyze /tmp/run.trace --output /tmp/analysis.html
3. Compare against baseline: 
   - ri-profiler compare /tmp/analysis.html --baseline /bench/baselines/<gpu-family>-baseline.html
4. If regression correlates with kernel A: enable conservative kernel fallback and roll a canary.

Detailed steps
- Step 1: Record request-level metadata with sample prompts and sequence-length distribution (include top-100 request IDs).
- Step 2: Export per-GPU utilization metrics (SM%, memBW, IPC) via telemetry: prometheus query node_exporter_gpu_sm_utilization{pool="<pool-id>"}.
- Step 3: Inspect kernel-level counters: average threads/warp, shared mem stall cycles, and achieved occupancy.
- Step 4: If increased queueing latency is the root cause, adjust batching_max_delay_ms and re-run profiling.

Common signatures and actions
- Symptom: high kernel launch latency + low occupancy -> action: enable larger micro-batches or switch to fused kernels.
- Symptom: sustained SM saturation (>95%) and high p99 latency -> action: autoscale (burst capacity) or shift non-critical traffic to lower-cost pools.

4) Benchmarking suite (canonical workload and reproducibility)

Overview
We keep a canonical benchmarking harness used for: model onboarding, release verification, and capacity planning. Benchmarks are reproducible via the bench-runner utility and stored baselines live in /bench/baselines.

Benchmark categories
- Latency (p50/p95/p99) using representative prompt sets (short, medium, long).
- Throughput (tokens/s) under steady-state load with warm KV-caches.
- Memory pressure tests: long-context runs to exercise eviction and memory allocation paths.
- Mixed workloads: concurrency and variable-length mixture to simulate production traffic.

Example benchmark command
- bench-runner run --model redwood/opt-6.7b --pool 8xA100 --workload mixed --duration 600 --warmup 120 --trace /tmp/bench.trace

Baseline storage and validation
- Baselines stored as HTML + JSON in /bench/baselines/<gpu-family>/<model>-<date>.
- CI gate: PRs touching runtime must not regress p95 latency by > 10% on the canonical benchmark (see CI plugin: bench-check).

Interpreting results
- Use the bench-diff tool to compare current run vs baseline: bench-diff /tmp/run.json /bench/baselines/8xA100/opt-6.7b-2026-01-10.json
- Key columns: delta p50/p95/p99, delta tokens/s, and memory high-water mark.

5) Release notes (selected recent entries)

2026-02-15 — v2026.02.15 (runtime-stable)
- Merged: improved kernel selector for short sequences (flash + int8 path).
- Fix: reduced token-level memory leaks on repeated streaming requests (ticket #SR-4813).
- Perf: p95 latency reduced 8% on opt-6.7b workloads.

2025-11-03 — v2025.11.03 (runtime-stable)
- Feature: KV cache elastic eviction (config kv_cache_elastic_eviction).
- Improvement: better telemetry for per-request trace ids.

2025-06-24 — v2025.06.24 (canary)
- Experiment: ROPE caching improvements for long-context handling.

6) Known issues and mitigations (triage-ready)

Issue SR-5220: Occasional fallback to CPU for quantized matmul on A100 with driver 525.x
- Symptom: sudden spike in latency (p99) on int8 models after driver update.
- Mitigation: pin driver to 520.61.05 until vendor patch. Rollback steps in runbook below.

Issue SR-4891: KV-cache thrash under bursty small requests
- Symptom: cache eviction churn and increased host-device traffic.
- Mitigation: enable kv_cache_elastic_eviction, increase cache-hot-window to 60s, and reduce batching_max_delay_ms to 3ms for low-latency lanes.

Issue SR-4708: Probe requests bypassing rate limiter under proxy failover
- Symptom: transient user-facing 429 then 503.
- Mitigation: add sticky routing for probe headers and increase proxy healthcheck stability.

7) Runtime runbooks (playbooks for incidents)

Runbook A: p99 latency regression (hosted API)
1. Acknowledge page and gather initial signals (last 15 minutes):
   - Alert page contains pool-id and topology.
2. Check router throttles and recent deploys: /dash/deploys?since=1h.
3. Run quick trace: ri-profiler capture --pool <pool-id> --duration 120 --out /tmp/quick.trace
4. If kernel stalls are present, enable conservative kernel fallback: 
   - ri-runtimectl set kernel_policy conservative --pool <pool-id> --duration 15m --reason "p99 regression"
5. If fallback reduces p99 by >20%, create a rollback or patch PR with telemetry.
6. Post-incident: run full profiler and add findings to postmortem.

Runbook B: GPU driver regression causing CPU fallbacks
1. Identify driver version via node exporter: node_gpu_driver_version.
2. If driver == 525.x and symptom matches SR-5220, mark pool NOMINATE_FOR_ROLLBACK and notify infra-ops.
3. Rollback steps: follow infra-runbook "driver-rollback-520-apply" (link in related pages).

Runbook C: KV-cache evictions causing throughput drop
1. Check kv-cache hit rate: prometheus query runtime_kv_cache_hit_ratio{pool="<pool>"}.
2. If hit ratio < 0.6 under steady-state, increase cache size or enable elastic eviction: ri-runtimectl set kv_cache_elastic_eviction true --pool <pool>.
3. Re-run bench-runner mixed workload for 10 minutes to confirm improvement.

8) Team wiki and onboarding notes

What new joiners need to know
- Read the runtime architecture doc and the profiling playbook top-to-bottom.
- Run the beginner benchmark: bench-runner run --model redwood/opt-1.3b --pool 1xA100 --duration 300 --warmup 60
- Shadow on-call for two weeks and perform one guided profiling exercise.

Useful links and artifacts
- Bench baselines: /bench/baselines/
- CI bench-check plugin docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/bench-check-plugin
- Kernel selector matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-selector-matrix

Appendix: sample configs and snippets

Example runtime config (YAML snippet)
| property | value | notes |
| batching_max_delay_ms | 6 | default for mixed workloads |
| batching_max_tokens | 16384 | safe default for 8xA100 pools |
| short_seq_thresh | 64 | favors flash kernels below this |
| occupancy_block_threshold | 0.91 | conservative kernel trigger |

CLI quick commands
- Capture profiler: ri-profiler capture --pool <pool-id> --duration 300 --out /tmp/run.trace
- Analyze trace: ri-profiler analyze /tmp/run.trace --output /tmp/analysis.html
- Set runtime knobs temporarily: ri-runtimectl set batching_max_delay_ms 4 --pool <pool-id> --duration 30m

Change log and maintenance
- This page is updated with every major runtime release and significant postmortems. Maintainers must update the Release notes section and append a one-line summary to the internal release digest.

FAQ (short)
Q: When should I increase batching_max_delay_ms?
A: When throughput is more important than latency (e.g., nightly ingest jobs), and p99 latency allowances exist.

Q: How do I test a kernel change safely?
A: Run the change in canary pools with bench-runner mixed workloads, check bench-diff against baseline, and run a 24-hour run to measure long-tail effects.
